name: Admata
title: One of the seven princes and advisors of the Persian king
summary: Admata was one of the seven princes in Persia and Media who had direct access to King Ahasuerus (Xerxes I). These seven wise men were the king's closest advisors, with special privileges at court, and knew the law and justice. They were consulted when Queen Vashti refused to obey the king's command to appear at his banquet. Admata is mentioned only by name in the list of these princes, and it is Memukan who speaks up and proposes the consequences for Vashti's disobedience.

keyEvents.title: Advisor at the Persian court
keyEvents.description: Admata was one of the seven princes in Persia and Media who held the highest positions in the empire and sat closest to the king. They had the right to see the king's face and knew the laws and customs of the time.

keyEvents.title: Vashti's disobedience and counsel
keyEvents.description: When Queen Vashti refused to come to King Ahasuerus' feast, the king sought advice from his seven princes, including Admata, on what should be done with her according to the law. Memukan, one of the seven, spoke up and proposed that Vashti should lose her position as queen, a counsel the king followed.

versions.title: One of the Persian king's seven counselors
versions.reason: [minor] The role 'leader' is somewhat general. 'Advisor' or 'prince' would be more precise, as Admata was specifically one of the seven princes/advisors at the Persian court. 'Wise man' is adequate, but 'prince' should be included to reflect his official title.; [minor] The four key events overlap somewhat in content. Event 1 and 3 cover similar themes (his position and knowledge of the law). These could usefully be combined to avoid repetition, though this is not an error.; [major] Footnotes are missing. For a Persian court official, it would be interesting to include historical context about the seven advisors in Persian tradition, as well as linguistic background for the name Admata.

footnotes.text: The name Admata (Hebrew: אַדְמָתָא) is likely of Persian origin. The exact etymology is debated, but it may be related to Old Iranian and mean 'unbound' or 'undefeated'. The name appears only in Esther 1:14.

The seven princes in Persia and Media mentioned in Esther 1:14 reflect a historically known practice in the Persian Achaemenid Empire. The Greek historian Herodotus (Histories 3.84) mentions seven Persian noble families that had special privileges and direct access to the king, which aligns well with the description in the book of Esther.

In Persian administration, the king's closest advisors functioned as a kind of royal council. Their role included legal advice, interpretation of laws and customs, and they had the right to enter unannounced before the king. This privilege ('to see the king's face') was highly sought after and limited to a small circle.

The rabbinic tradition has not given Admata special attention, as he is mentioned only by name in the list of the seven princes. However, in Targum Sheni to the book of Esther, expanded descriptions are provided of the seven counselors and their functions at the court.
